title: Anthropometric Measurements Inform Complete Concentric Collapse Status in Patients With Obstructive Sleep Apnea
authors: Weiner JS, Chio EG, Dedhia RC, Huntley CT, Hutz MJ, Huyett P, et al.
blurb: A prospective multicenter study asked whether body mass index, neck circumference and awake pharyngeal width can predict complete concentric collapse on drug-induced sleep endoscopy in candidates for hypoglossal nerve stimulation. A decision tree combining body mass index and neck circumference was right 96 percent of the time when it predicted no collapse, only modestly better than assuming no one has it, and the study reported no implant outcomes. Sleep endoscopy remains the standard for candidacy, and this screening approach is one to watch. The study was funded by Inspire Medical Systems.

title: Deep Learning-Based Automatic Scoring of Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy in Obstructive Sleep Apnea
authors: Kim JY, Mun SJ, Baik YS, Lee YS, Kim YJ, Oh J, et al.
blurb: A five-hospital Korean study asked whether a deep learning model could grade drug-induced sleep endoscopy videos the way an expert panel does, scoring both the degree of airway obstruction and its primary cause. On videos from hospitals not used in training, the model matched expert grading of soft palate obstruction in 82.4 percent of 717 clips, with weaker performance lower in the airway, especially at the epiglottis. It is a tool to watch: it cannot grade concentric collapse and has not been linked to treatment outcomes, so it does not yet inform hypoglossal nerve stimulation candidacy.

title: Subjective and objective measures of sleep-related function from the Cardiovascular Endpoints For Obstructive Sleep Apnea with Twelfth Cranial Nerve Stimulation (CARDIOSA-12) trial: Sleep-related functional outcomes in CARDIOSA-12
authors: Tangutur A, Yu PK, Basner M, Keenan BT, Dedhia RC.
blurb: A secondary analysis of the Cardiovascular Endpoints for Obstructive Sleep Apnea with Twelfth Cranial Nerve Stimulation (CARDIOSA-12) randomized crossover trial asked whether full versus partial hypoglossal nerve stimulation improves objective cognition and patient-reported sleep outcomes in obstructive sleep apnea. Sleepiness, insomnia, snoring and daily-function questionnaire scores improved on full stimulation, with the Epworth sleepiness score about 1.75 points lower, but reaction-time and processing-speed tests showed no statistically significant difference in the main analysis. The findings leave candidacy as it was but support counseling patients to expect feeling better, not measurably sharper thinking.

title: Three-Year Outcomes of Proximal Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation in OSA
authors: Schwartz AR, Jacobowitz O, Mickelson SA, Miller MB, Oliven A, Certal V, et al.
blurb: Schwartz and colleagues, with Maurer as senior author, asked whether proximal hypoglossal nerve stimulation, a LivaNova device distinct from Inspire, keeps working at three years in the Targeted Hypoglossal Neurostimulation 3 trial. In the patients who completed a three-year sleep study, the median apnea-hypopnea index was roughly halved and held steady from year one, though about one in four patients did not finish follow-up and no three-year responder rate was reported. Take-home point: useful counseling evidence for patients asking about the other nerve stimulator, but not a reason to change Inspire candidacy criteria.

title: Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation and Hypoxic Burden in Patients With Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Secondary Analysis of the STAR Trial
authors: Xu J, Hajipour Z, Aloia MS, de Beeck SO, Vanderveken OM, Huyett P, et al.
blurb: A secondary analysis of the Stimulation Therapy for Apnea Reduction trial asked whether hypoglossal nerve stimulation with a first-generation Inspire device lowers hypoxic burden, a measure of how deep and how long nighttime oxygen drops are. About seven in ten patients had their hypoxic burden cut by more than half at one year, though the study had no control group and measured no heart events. The finding is one to watch and adds a useful counseling point, but it does not change who is offered implantation.

title: Proximal Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation for Obstructive Sleep Apnea in the OSPREY Study: A Randomized Controlled Trial
authors: Malhotra A, Schwartz AR, Lovett E, Juran N, Nguyen SA, Barrera JE, et al.
blurb: The OSPREY randomized trial tested whether an investigational proximal hypoglossal nerve stimulator, the LivaNova aura6000, works better than the same device implanted but switched off in adults with moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea who could not tolerate positive airway pressure. At seven months, 58.2 percent of 67 treated patients met the response criteria, compared with 13.5 percent of 37 controls, with no serious device-related adverse events. The trial gives surgeons a randomized benchmark for counseling patients about an investigational alternative, but it is not Inspire evidence and does not address complete concentric collapse, so it is one to watch.

title: A Randomized Trial of Nefopam for Postoperative Pain Management in Obstructive Sleep Apnea Patients Undergoing Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty
authors: Chumpathong S, Mangmeesri P, Panyamee S, Banhiran W, Uataya M.
blurb: Chumpathong and colleagues at Siriraj Hospital in Bangkok ran a small randomized, placebo-controlled trial asking whether nefopam, a non-opioid pain drug not approved in the United States, reduces morphine use in the first day after uvulopalatopharyngoplasty for obstructive sleep apnea. Added to a strong multimodal pain regimen, it did not: both groups needed only a few milligrams of morphine, with no statistically significant difference. Because the trial was underpowered, it supports not adding nefopam routinely while leaving a modest effect unexcluded.

title: Systematic Review on the Safety of Outpatient Upper Airway Surgery for Obstructive Sleep Apnea Patients in Ambulatory Surgical Centers
authors: Asghar M, Pang K, Asghar M, Rotenberg B.
journal: Journal of Otolaryngology - Head & Neck Surgery
blurb: A 2025 systematic review from Rotenberg's group asked whether adults with obstructive sleep apnea can safely have nasal and palate surgery in ambulatory surgical centers and go home the same day. Across mostly older, hospital-based studies, unplanned admission for medical reasons averaged 5.4 percent across the four studies that reported it, above the authors' own 3 percent benchmark, and serious events were rare and came within the first few hours. The take-home point: the review maps early risk usefully but contains almost no true surgery-center data, so it does not yet justify moving pharyngoplasty patients out of overnight observation.

title: Association Between Perioperative Celecoxib, Acetaminophen, and Opioid Consumption After Palate Surgery for Obstructive Sleep Apnea
authors: Badash I, Wong S, Biju K, Hur K, Commesso E, Kezirian EJ.
blurb: A single-surgeon retrospective study by Badash and colleagues, with Kezirian as senior author, asked whether celecoxib or acetaminophen given around palate surgery for obstructive sleep apnea was associated with less opioid use in the first day after surgery. Higher celecoxib doses were associated with modestly lower opioid use, while acetaminophen showed no significant association, and 205 of 210 patients still received opioids. Because celecoxib became routine partway through the study period, the finding is one to watch for confirmation in a randomized trial.

title: Predictive Factors for Surgical Outcomes and Symptom Persistence After Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty in Patients With Obstructive Sleep Apnea
authors: Ling X, Zheng J, Liu Q, Shi C, Fan C.
blurb: A single-center study from Wujin Hospital in China asked which preoperative features predict success after a modified uvulopalatopharyngoplasty for obstructive sleep apnea. About two in three patients met the success definition at short-term follow-up, and a lower Friedman stage, lower body mass index and higher lowest oxygen saturation were linked to success. The proposed prediction model has not been validated outside the patients who built it, so it is one to watch.

title: Uvularis Muscle Strengthening Advancement in Palatopharyngeal Collapse in Selected Cases of Snoring and Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Randomized Trial
authors: Askar SM, Awad AM, Abou-Sharkh AA.
blurb: A randomized trial from Zagazig University in Egypt asked whether adding a uvularis muscle advancement stitch to modified anterior palatoplasty improves outcomes in young adults with mild or early moderate obstructive sleep apnea and single-level, front-to-back palatal collapse. In 34 patients, the added stitch did not significantly lower the apnea-hypopnea index compared with palatoplasty alone, although bed-partner-rated snoring improved more. The snoring benefit is one to watch, pending a blinded, registered trial.

title: Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty Versus Expansion Sphincter Pharyngoplasty - A Single Centre Experience
authors: Steinbichler TB, Bender B, Hartl R, Strasser V, Sontheimer D, Buricic S, et al.
blurb: A retrospective single-center study from the Medical University of Innsbruck compared expansion sphincter pharyngoplasty with a muscle-sparing uvulopalatopharyngoplasty in patients with snoring or obstructive sleep apnea, with the operation chosen by drug-induced sedation endoscopy findings. Expansion sphincter pharyngoplasty significantly lowered the apnea-hypopnea index, to about 13 events per hour, while the uvulopalatopharyngoplasty group's fall was not significant; expansion sphincter pharyngoplasty also brought more minor bleeding and more strong pain medication. The study adds independent support for palate operations that reshape the lateral pharyngeal wall and gives frank morbidity numbers for counseling, but it cannot prove superiority and does not test barbed reposition pharyngoplasty.

title: Auditory Perceptions Associated With Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation for Obstructive Sleep Apnea
authors: Belilos A, Adibi I, Tucker A, Saeedi A, Calder A, Lee L, Nord R.
blurb: Researchers at Virginia Commonwealth University surveyed Inspire hypoglossal nerve stimulation recipients by telephone to ask whether they hear new sounds when the device stimulates. About one in six reported a new buzzing or humming sound during stimulation, mostly mild, and none had stopped using the device; preexisting tinnitus was not a statistically significant predictor in this small sample. The finding changes how patients are counseled and questioned about sound at follow-up, not who is offered the implant.

title: Preservation Palatopharyngoplasty for Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Predictors and Clinical Outcomes
authors: Abdelwahab M, Alhussien A, Kassir MF, Butehorn H, Munhall C, Nguyen SA.
blurb: A single-surgeon retrospective series from the Medical University of South Carolina asked how adults with moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea fare after preservation palatopharyngoplasty, and which baseline features predict a larger drop in the apnea-hypopnea index. The apnea-hypopnea index was cut roughly in half, with larger tonsils and higher baseline severity predicting bigger drops, though only a minority of patients were cured. The take-home point: the paper sharpens counseling for patients with large tonsils who fall outside Inspire candidacy, but it needs controlled, longer-term confirmation.

title: Post-Operative Radiological Evaluation of a Bilateral Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation System
authors: Kilgue A, Gehl H-B, Abolmaali N, Scholtz L-U, Scherl C, Todt I.
blurb: A single-center German case series of eleven patients asked what the first postoperative image should be after implanting the Genio bilateral hypoglossal nerve stimulator. Plain x-rays showed the hardware cleanly in every patient, while every computed tomography scan carried metal artifact, and the paper reported no clinical outcomes linking paddle position to function. The take-home point: plain films make a sensible day-one baseline, and repeat imaging over time is needed to show whether the paddles migrate.

title: Exploring the Role of Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy in Optimizing Upper Airway Stimulation Therapy for Non-Responders
authors: Kant E, Hardeman JA, Stokroos RJ, Copper MP.
blurb: Copper's group at Sint Antonius Hospital in the Netherlands described how they use drug-induced sleep endoscopy with the stimulator switched on in patients who still fail Inspire hypoglossal nerve stimulation after standard titration, and what happened to those patients afterwards. In a small retrospective series without a control group, patients who had settings changes or added therapy and returned for follow-up saw their apnea-hypopnea index fall by about 18 events per hour. Dr. Nord considers the procedure a good tool for the tolerant non-responder once awake endoscopy and reprogramming have failed, while noting that the series cannot show the endoscopy itself caused the improvement.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists for obstructive sleep apnea: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
authors: Carvalhal G, Mora MMR, Peralta-Jiménez GA, Ayasa L, Barrera V, Advani K, et al.
blurb: A meta-analysis in Sleep and Breathing pooled randomized trials of liraglutide and tirzepatide in adults with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea. The drugs lowered the apnea-hypopnea index by about ten events per hour more than control, but the effect depended heavily on the drug, and pooled oxygen measures did not improve significantly. The paper does not change who is offered surgery, but it sharpens counseling: quote drug-specific numbers, re-test after weight loss, and, as in Dr. Nord's practice, treat weight-loss drugs and Inspire as complementary parts of treatment, though no trial has yet tested them together.

title: Edema and Subjective Discomfort After Barbed Stayed Bridge Pharyngoplasty (BSBP)
authors: Pace A, Iannella G, Maniaci A, Cocuzza S, Moffa A, Alunni Fegatelli D, et al.
blurb: Researchers at Sapienza University of Rome followed a small, carefully selected group of patients with moderate obstructive sleep apnea after barbed stayed bridge pharyngoplasty, a muscle-sparing barbed palate operation, to measure early pain, swelling and discomfort. Pain stayed low, averaging about three out of ten on the first day and near zero by one month, with no bleeding, but without a comparison group the study cannot show the technique outperforms barbed reposition pharyngoplasty. Dr. Nord's take-home point: a promising early-recovery signal for one technique in thirty selected patients, still awaiting a head-to-head comparison with barbed reposition pharyngoplasty.

title: Hypoxic Burden Reduction After Lateral Pharyngoplasty in Patients With Obstructive Sleep Apnea - Beyond the Apnea-Hypopnea Index
authors: Vieira ALP, Duarte BB, Almeida AR, Greters ME, Leandro-Merhi VA, de Aquino JLB.
blurb: A single-center study from the Pontifical Catholic University of Campinas in Brazil asked whether lateral pharyngoplasty lowers hypoxic burden, a measure of nighttime oxygen loss, and not just the apnea-hypopnea index. In the 27 patients with hypoxic burden measured before and after surgery, median hypoxic burden fell to about a third of baseline. It also fell significantly in patients who failed by apnea-hypopnea index criteria, but the study had no control group and measured no cardiovascular outcomes. Verdict: watch — it supports reporting hypoxic burden alongside the apnea-hypopnea index after palate surgery, without changing who is offered surgery.

title: Ultrasonographic Tongue Base Motion Does Not Correlate With Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Outcomes
authors: Tschopp S, Janjic V, Caversaccio M, Borner U, Tschopp K.
blurb: A two-center Swiss study asked whether the way the tongue base moves on awake ultrasound during hypoglossal nerve stimulation predicts how much a patient's obstructive sleep apnea improves. In 64 patients with unilateral Inspire implants, no ultrasound measure of tongue movement size, symmetry or shape was significantly associated with the drop in the apnea-hypopnea index, though the confidence intervals were wide. The call is no change in practice, with ultrasound worth watching as a research tool.

title: Oropharyngeal Lateral Wall Collapse on Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy as a Predictor of Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Response in Obstructive Sleep Apnoea-A Systematic Review
authors: McBrinn S, Skan O, Iacovidou A.
blurb: A systematic review of eight Inspire cohorts, 1,051 patients in all, asked whether complete collapse of the lateral pharyngeal walls on sleep endoscopy predicts a poor response to hypoglossal nerve stimulation. It lowers the response rate by roughly 15 to 20 percentage points, yet about two of three such patients still respond, so it is a counseling point rather than an exclusion. Call: watch.

title: Consensus Statements Among European Sleep Surgery Experts on Tongue, Hypopharynx, and Supraglottis Associated With Snoring and Obstructive Sleep Apnea - Part 1 - Evaluation and Decision Making
authors: Olszewska E, De Vito A, Baptista P, Delakorda M, Heiser C, Cheong RCT, et al.
blurb: A European expert panel reached consensus on how to evaluate the tongue base, hypopharynx and supraglottis in snoring and sleep apnea, and how those findings should steer treatment. The statements support staging palate surgery before hypoglossal nerve stimulation when large tonsils coexist with tongue base collapse, and repeating sleep endoscopy before any revision surgery. Call: watch; the workup stays as it is.
